title: Chapter 108 — Ahab and the Carpenter
paragraphs: The Deck — First Night Watch.

(The carpenter stands at his vise-bench, filing away busily by the light of two lanterns at the ivory shaft for the leg, which is clamped tight in the vise. Slabs of ivory, leather straps, pads, screws and all kinds of tools lie scattered over the bench. Farther forward the red flame of the forge can be seen, where the blacksmith is working.)

Drat the file, and drat the bone! What should be soft is hard, and what should be hard is soft. That's how it goes for us who file old jaws and shinbones. Let's try another. Aye, now, this works better (sneezes). Hello, this bone dust is (sneezes) — why it's (sneezes) — yes it's (sneezes) — bless my soul, it won't let me speak! This is what an old fellow gets now for working in dead lumber. Saw a live tree and you don't get this dust; amputate a live bone and you don't get it (sneezes). Come, come, you old Smut, there, lend a hand, and let's have that ferrule and buckle-screw; I'll be ready for them in a minute. Lucky now (sneezes) there's no knee-joint to make; that might puzzle me a little; but a mere shinbone — why, it's as easy as making hop-poles; only I'd like to put a good finish on it. Time, time; if I only had the time, I could turn him out as neat a leg now as ever (sneezes) scraped to a lady in a parlor. Those buckskin legs and calves I've seen in shop windows wouldn't compare at all. They soak up water, they do; and of course they get rheumatic and have to be doctored (sneezes) with washes and lotions, just like live legs. There; before I saw it off, now, I must call his old Mogulship and see whether the length will be all right; too short, if anything, I guess. Ha! That's the heel; we're in luck; here he comes, or it's somebody else, that's certain.
AHAB (advancing). (During the ensuing scene, the carpenter continues sneezing at times.)
Well, man-maker!
Just in time, sir. If it suits the captain, I'll mark the length now. Let me measure you, sir.

Measured for a leg! Good. Well, it's not the first time. Get to it! There; keep your finger on it. This is a strong vise you have here, carpenter; let me feel its grip once. So, so; it does pinch some.
Oh, sir, it will break bones — beware, beware!
Don't worry; I like a good grip. I like to feel something in this slippery world that can hold on, man. What's Prometheus up to over there? The blacksmith, I mean — what's he doing?
He must be forging the buckle-screw, sir, now.
Right. It's a partnership; he supplies the muscle part. He makes a fierce red flame there!
Aye, sir; he must have the white heat for this kind of fine work.

Mm. So he must. It strikes me now as deeply significant that the old Greek Prometheus, who made men, so they say, should have been a blacksmith and brought them to life with fire; for whatever is made in fire must rightly belong to fire, and so hell is likely. Look how the soot flies! This must be the leftover stuff the Greek made the Africans from. Carpenter, when he's finished with that buckle, tell him to forge a pair of steel shoulder blades; there's a peddler on board with a crushing pack.
Sir?

Wait. While Prometheus is at it, I'll order a complete man, made to a pattern I like. Item one: fifty feet tall in his socks. Next, a chest built on the model of the Thames Tunnel. Next, legs with roots on them, so he stays in one place. Next, arms three feet thick at the wrist. No heart at all, a brass forehead, and about a quarter of an acre of fine brains. And let me see — shall I order eyes that look outward? No, but put a skylight on top of his head to light up the inside. There, take the order and be off.
Now what is he talking about, and who is he talking to, I'd like to know? Should I keep standing here? (aside)
It is poor architecture to make a blind dome; here's one. No, no, no; I must have a lantern.
Ho, ho! That's it, hey? Here are two, sir; one will do for me.
What are you thrusting that thief-catcher into my face for, man? Forced light is worse than pointed pistols.
I thought, sir, that you spoke to the carpenter.
Carpenter? Why, that's — but no; a very tidy, and, I may say, an extremely gentlemanlike sort of business you are in here, carpenter; or would you rather work in clay?
Sir? Clay? Clay, sir? That's mud; we leave clay to ditchers, sir.
The fellow's impious! What are you sneezing about?
Bone is rather dusty, sir.
Take the hint, then; and when you are dead, never bury yourself under living people's noses.
Sir? Oh! Ah! I guess so; yes — oh, dear!

Look here, carpenter, I daresay you call yourself a right good workmanlike workman, eh? Well, then, will it speak thoroughly well for your work if, when I come to mount this leg you make, I shall nevertheless feel another leg in the same identical place with it; that is, carpenter, my old lost leg; the flesh and blood one, I mean. Can you not drive that old Adam away?

Well, sir, I'm starting to understand a little now. Yes, I've heard something curious about that, sir: that a dismasted man never quite loses the feeling of his old spar, and it still pricks him now and then. May I humbly ask if that's really true, sir?

It is, man. Look, put your living leg here, in the spot where mine used to be. There — now the eye sees only one distinct leg, but the soul sees two. Where you feel tingling life, there, exactly there, right down to a hair, I feel it too. Is that a riddle?
I should humbly call it a puzzler, sir.

Hush, then. How do you know that some entire, living, thinking thing may not be standing invisibly, and without mingling with you, exactly where you are standing now; aye, and standing there in spite of you? In your most solitary hours, then, don't you fear eavesdroppers? Hold on, don't speak! And if I still feel the sting of my crushed leg, though it has now been dissolved so long, then why might you not, carpenter, feel the fiery pains of hell forever, and without a body? Hah!
Good Lord! Honestly, sir, if it comes to that, I'll have to work out my sums again; I think I forgot to carry a small figure, sir.
Look here, pudding-heads should never grant premises. How long before the leg is done?
Perhaps an hour, sir.

Bungle away at it, then, and bring it to me when it's done (turns to go). Oh, Life! Here I stand, as proud as a Greek god, and yet I am in debt to this blockhead for a bone to stand on! A curse on this mortal web of everyone owing everyone, which will never let us be rid of ledgers. I want to be as free as air, and here I am written down in the whole world's account books. I am so rich that I could have matched the wealthiest Praetorians bid for bid when they auctioned off the Roman empire (which was the world's); and yet I owe for the very flesh of the tongue I brag with. By heaven! I'll get a crucible, climb in, and melt myself down into one small, compact vertebra. So.
CARPENTER (resuming his work).

Well, well, well! Stubb knows him best of all, and Stubb always says he's queer; says nothing but that one sufficient little word queer; he's queer, says Stubb; he's queer — queer, queer; and keeps dinning it into Mr. Starbuck all the time — queer, sir, queer, queer, very queer. And here's his leg! Yes, now that I think of it, here's his bedfellow! Has a stick of whale's jawbone for a wife! And this is his leg; he'll stand on this. What was that now about one leg standing in three places, and all three places standing in one hell — how was that? Oh! I don't wonder he looked so scornful at me! I'm sort of strange-thoughted sometimes, they say; but that's only haphazard-like. Then, a short little old body like me should never try to wade out into deep waters with tall, heron-built captains; the water chucks you under the chin pretty quick, and there's a great cry for lifeboats. And here's the heron's leg! Long and slim, sure enough! Now, for most folks one pair of legs lasts a lifetime, and that must be because they use them mercifully, the way a tender-hearted old lady uses her roly-poly old coach-horses. But Ahab — oh, he's a hard driver. Look, he's driven one leg to death and lamed the other for life, like a spavined horse, and now wears out bone legs by the cord. Hello, there, you Smut! Lend a hand there with those screws, and let's finish it before the resurrection fellow comes calling with his horn for all legs, true or false, the way brewery-men go round collecting old beer barrels to fill them up again. What a leg this is! It looks like a real live leg, filed down to nothing but the core; he'll be standing on this tomorrow; he'll be taking altitudes on it. Hello! I almost forgot the little oval slate, smoothed ivory, where he figures up the latitude. So, so; chisel, file, and sandpaper, now!
